memory_text: During Dashain, our family receives tika and jamara from the eldest person. The blessing matters more than the feast: it reconnects relatives who have walked back to the village from far away.
Yomari is made from fresh rice flour shaped like a fish and filled with chaku and sesame. We prepare it during Yomari Punhi to thank the harvest and share the first batch with neighbours.

Before sowing rice, we watched the flowering of the simal tree and listened for frogs after the first warm rain. Seedlings were exchanged between households so one failed nursery would not ruin a family's year.
In Indra Jatra, the masked Lakhey is not simply a demon. Elders told us he became a protector of children, and his fierce dance clears the street while the community gathers.

Our hill spring was said to have appeared where a tired traveller struck the earth with a walking stick. Whether miracle or memory, nobody washed clothes at its source; the story protected clean drinking water.
We say 'thuchi che' to offer thanks. Children were taught to say it not only to people but quietly after receiving food or shelter, as a habit of gratitude.

A bamboo doko is woven from the base upward. My father taught by letting my hands make loose crossings first, then undoing them with me; a strong basket came after learning not to fear starting again.
